comment.value:
CSI-Bench is a large-scale in-the-wild dataset for multi-task WiFi sensing. It contains diverse sensing scenarios, multiple chipsets, and multiple tasks, making it the first dataset of this scope in the area. The authors also provide baselines and analyses that demonstrate the utility of CSI-Bench as a benchmark for future research.

Reviewers appreciated the novelty and relevance of the contribution, highlighting the dataset’s scale, diversity, and potential to support a wide range of applications. In the rebuttal, the authors clarified some details about dataset collection, labeling, and task design, which resolved most reviewer concerns. The discussion confirmed that the contribution is solid and timely. Many additional information is promised to be provided by the authors (e.g. phase data).

Some limitations remain, such as the absence of even broader coverage of sensing environments and the inclusion of additional tasks. However, at some point this  would also be beyond the scope of a single paper.

All reviewers vote for acceptance. Overall, I recommend acceptance. The dataset fills an important gap, offers clear utility for advancing multi-task WiFi sensing, and is expected to have meaningful impact by enabling new research directions in this area, in particular, making CSI more accessible to ML researchers.

author_final_remarks.value:
We thank all reviewers for their thoughtful evaluations and constructive suggestions. We are encouraged by the strong consensus that CSI-Bench represents a significant and timely contribution to WiFi sensing and human-centric AI research. Reviewers acknowledged our clear writing, strong experimental design, comprehensive task coverage, rigorous evaluation protocols (difficulty tiers and OOD settings), and its scale and diversity (461 hours, 35 users, 26 environments, 16 commercial devices) under realistic, hardware-diverse conditions.

Following the rebuttal and discussions, the positive feedback from all reviewers and their willingness to raise or maintain their scores reflect that our clarifications effectively addressed their concerns. This reaffirms the significance of CSI-Bench as the first large-scale, in-the-wild WiFi sensing benchmark enabling both single-task and multi-task learning across diverse devices and environments.

In response to the feedback, we clarified our rationale for focusing on amplitude-only CSI, detailed our robust device and environment selection strategy, and described the standardized preprocessing pipeline. We also committed to releasing raw phase data, continuous CSI traces, and additional users to support broader research directions, including phase-aware modeling, long-term structured tasks, and generalization studies. We addressed the “healthcare relevance” concern by articulating that all seven benchmark tasks are directly applicable to healthcare and assisted living, enabling continuous monitoring and timely intervention with privacy in mind. We conducted ablation studies on preprocessing, justified segmentation parameters, and emphasized that even tasks with high in-distribution accuracy expose substantial robustness gaps in real-world OOD scenarios.

CSI-Bench enables research previously infeasible: systematically quantifying generalization gaps across devices, users, and environments, and benchmarking scalable models deployable on existing commodity infrastructure. It bridges the lab-to-real-world gap in wireless sensing and opens new research directions in domain adaptation, robust representation learning, and foundation models for WiFi.  

We are confident that CSI-Bench will serve as a lasting resource for the ML and ubiquitous computing communities, with broad applicability to healthcare and beyond. We believe it merits acceptance and will foster continued advances in research and real-world deployment.

Thank you to the authors for their detailed responses. While all of my major concerns have been addressed, I would like to offer a few suggestions that could further enhance the readability and potential impact of this work:

1. For the healthcare-specific benchmarks, it would be helpful to include both conceptual figures illustrating how these tasks relate to and benefit healthcare applications, as well as the clear textual explanations mentioned in the rebuttal.  I believe incorporating these together into the revised version would make the contributions more accessible and meaningful to a broader audience.

2. Regarding the use of a single modality,  I fully understand and agree with the authors’ design choice, especially considering practicality, scalability, and privacy. Given the aims of this work, it is completely reasonable not to include additional modalities. However, I believe that incorporating additional modalities such as skeleton, text, or depth information could broaden the dataset’s applicability to other contactless human-centric tasks, including pose estimation and motion generation. This expansion could further enhance the dataset’s value and long-term impact within the human-centric healthcare research community.


Overall, I believe this work makes a valuable contribution to the field of WiFi-based human sensing for healthcare. Based on these points, I plan to raise my rating to "accept" in the final justification phase.

rebuttal.value:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful review and valuable feedback. We are encouraged by the recognition of our contributions—including the real-world heterogeneity, continuous recording pipeline, and strong potential for promoting generalizable WiFi sensing. We address each concern below and specify the improvements we will make in response.


**[L1] Healthcare-Specific Benchmarks:** We appreciate the reviewer’s concern and respectfully clarify that CSI-Bench supports healthcare applications beyond the two explicitly named “fall detection” and “breathing detection” tasks. Specifically, all seven tasks directly support critical healthcare applications:

- **Room-level localization** enables tracking patient movement patterns, detecting wandering behavior in dementia patients, ensuring post-surgery mobility compliance, and identifying meal-skipping behaviors via occupancy patterns in kitchens.
- **Proximity recognition** supports fall risk assessment by monitoring distance to support devices, medication adherence detection near pill dispensers, and social isolation monitoring.
- **Activity recognition** provides continuous behavioral monitoring for depression symptom detection, rehabilitation progress tracking, and early identification of health deterioration patterns.
- **User identification** enables multi-resident monitoring in assisted living facilities with privacy-compliant individual tracking and personalized emergency response.
- **Motion source recognition** differentiates human movement from pets/devices, crucial for accurate health monitoring and reducing false alarms in emergency detection systems.

These tasks collectively enable comprehensive smart health monitoring systems that detect early signs of cognitive decline, monitor chronic disease progression, and provide actionable caregiver insights—all through privacy-preserving contactless sensing.

These recordings are excluded from the current submission due to file size, standardization considerations, and NeurIPS restrictions on dataset modifications during review. The full-length data will enable regression tasks, continuous monitoring, and variable-length sequence modeling.


**[L3] Data Diversity in Breathing Detection:** We acknowledge that the current breathing detection dataset includes three users. However, we would like to clarify that our breathing detection dataset achieves exceptional diversity through systematic experimental design that prioritizes signal complexity over participant quantity:
- It spans three distinct environments and a wide range of signal conditions—from same-room line-of-sight to challenging cross-room **non-line-of-sight** setups, with distances ranging from 0.5 to 3.5 m and device heights from **0.47 m (power socket) to 2.18 m (ceiling)**.
- Breathing sessions were recorded in both sleep and non-sleep states to capture physiological variability across postures and time.
- The dataset includes **~55,000 breathing samples**, along with **~11,400 fan-interfered samples**, reflecting the high task complexity and signal sensitivity involved in this scenario.

Despite the limited number of users, the diversity in settings and noise conditions makes the task **non-trivial**, with performance varying significantly across settings. Our approach prioritizes signal quality and scenario diversity over participant quantity, providing a benchmark for robust respiration sensing.

We thank the reviewer for the suggestion and agree that expanding user diversity is also valuable. In fact, our co-labeled multi-task dataset also includes breathing samples for *seated-breathing* activity from 6 users, and we have recently collected additional data from 4 more users, including 2 children. We will integrate these into the dataset and enhance the breathing evaluation in the camera-ready version.


**[L4] Multi-task Dataset Scale:** We thank the reviewer for highlighting the importance of diversity in generalization studies. While the current co-labeled multi-task dataset includes 6 users, 6 environments, and 11 device types, it is already significantly more diverse than prior WiFi sensing datasets (Table 1). More importantly, we carefully selected these to ensure diversity across:
- **User demographics**: Participants span ages 26–41 and body weights 45–90kg, as detailed in Appendix Table 5.

- **Environment types**: From compact apartments (633 sqft) to large homes (2600 sqft), introducing varied occlusion, multipath, and layout factors.

- **Device hardware**: 11 device types span all major commercial chipset vendors and configurations currently dominating the IoT market, representing a broad range of chipsets, antenna setups, and bandwidths (Table 6), covering 2.4/5 GHz and 20/40/80 MHz modes.

Importantly, the substantial performance drops in our OOD evaluation (Appendix C.2) demonstrate that our current scale provides meaningful generalization challenges that will drive future research innovation. 


**[L5] Preprocessing Strategy Analysis:** We acknowledge that preprocessing strategy analysis would provide valuable insights, and we can address this constructively within our current work scope.

In the current version, we adopt a minimal yet standardized preprocessing pipeline, comprising global amplitude normalization, subcarrier alignment, and antenna concatenation, not to optimize performance but to ensure consistency across the heterogeneous hardware and environments covered in CSI-Bench. This design choice enables fair comparison across models and settings and provides a stable, reproducible foundation for future exploration. We aim for our dataset to serve as a community resource that supports systematic study of various preprocessing strategies at scale.

To directly address this point, we conducted an ablation study on the Fall Detection task using the Transformer model. We compared the downstream performance under three normalization settings: the default CSI-Bench amplitude normalization (per-segment), no normalization, and per-subcarrier normalization. Results on the in-distribution split are shown below:
| Normalization Type            | Accuracy (%) | F1 Score (%) |
| ----------------------------- | ------------ | ------------ |
| Per-segment (CSI-Bench)       | **94.28**    | **94.26**    |
| No normalization              | 93.03        | 92.96        |
| Per-subcarrier normalization | 86.37        | 86.49        |

The standardized per-segment normalization used in CSI-Bench yields the best overall performance, outperforming both alternatives by up to +1.25% in accuracy and F1. This validates our design choice for providing a reliable evaluation baseline.

We plan to include an expanded analysis in the final version, comparing additional preprocessing strategies (e.g., subcarrier alignment variants, antenna ordering) to further assess their impact on model performance. This complements our main contribution by highlighting CSI-Bench’s utility as a robust platform for evaluating not only models but also signal processing strategies.

**[F1] Phase Data Future Release:** We agree that calibrated phase can broaden applicability for localization and direction-of-arrival tasks. We plan to release raw phase data in the update version of CSI-Bench to support such work.

**[F2] Temporally Structured Tasks:**  We recognize the high practical value of long-term structured tasks. Our dataset includes overnight breathing sessions and continuous CSI recordings. We will release full-length recordings in the update version of CSI-Benchto support native long-term task formulation.

**[F3] API Development:** We appreciate this excellent suggestion to improve dataset usability. Our GitHub includes standardized HDF5 files and consistent data loading scripts, and we can easily add PyTorch and TensorFlow wrappers. Due to review restrictions, code updates aren’t allowed now, but we will prioritize comprehensive API support post-acceptance to ensure accessibility across frameworks and user preferences.

**[F4] Hardware Configuration Analysis:** We appreciate this valuable suggestion on hardware analysis. We already provide detailed device specs (Table 6) and cross-device results (Appendix C.2), showing that models like ResNet18 and ViT are more robust to hardware variation than sequence-based models. We can further break down performance by bandwidth (20/40/80 MHz), MIMO (1×1, 2×2), and frequency band (2.4/5 GHz), offering practical deployment insights. Our dataset’s hardware diversity uniquely enables this analysis, and we will expand it in the revised version to better guide real-world use.


We believe these enhancements address the concerns while strengthening CSI-Bench's contribution to the community. We thank the reviewer again for the thoughtful review and constructive suggestions.

summary.value: This paper introduces CSI-Bench, a large-scale in-the-wild benchmark dataset for multi-task WiFi sensing. The dataset comprises over 460 hours of Channel State Information (CSI) recordings collected from 35 real users, 26 diverse environments, and 16 commercial edge devices. CSI-Bench supports both single-task datasets (e.g., fall detection, breathing monitoring, localization, motion source recognition) and a co-labeled multi-task dataset (user identification, activity recognition, and proximity estimation). The paper also provides standardized data splits, multiple baselines, and demonstrates the benefits of multi-task learning for improved generalization and parameter efficiency.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The dataset spans 26 indoor environments (apartments, offices, homes, etc.) and 35 real users, utilizing 16 heterogeneous WiFi devices, reflecting the diversity and complexity of real-world deployments.

2. The dataset offers four single-task datasets and one co-labeled multi-task dataset, supporting tasks such as activity recognition, user identification, and proximity estimation, facilitating parameter-efficient shared learning

3. Training/validation/test splits are provided along with difficulty-level stratification (Easy/Medium/Hard) and OOD evaluation settings (cross-user, cross-environment, cross-device)

4. Experiments include MLP, LSTM, ResNet-18, Transformer, ViT, etc., and comparisons between single-task and multi-task learning, showing that multi-task learning can enhance performance and reduce parameter count by over 60%.

5. The paper is well-structured with clear writing. Figures and tables (e.g., Table 1 comparison, Figure 2 CSI patterns, Figure 3 device quality differences) are informative and easy to interpret.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The dataset seems to only provide CSI amplitude data, excluding many research directions that rely on calibrated phase or angle-of-arrival information, making it unsuitable for fine-grained localization and similar tasks.

2. The dataset is segmented into short-duration samples for classification tasks. It does not yet include regression or long-term activity tracking tasks, limiting its applicability for certain sensing scenarios.

3. The breathing detection dataset involves only 3 users (Table 5), which may lack representativeness and could lead to overfitting. Increasing user diversity is recommended.

4. The multi-task dataset covers only 6 users, 6 environments, and 11 device types (Table 2), which may be insufficient for generalization studies, especially under cross-user and cross-device settings.

5. Although preprocessing (e.g., amplitude normalization, subcarrier alignment) is described, the effects of different preprocessing strategies on downstream model performance are not quantitatively compared.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value:
1. All data were collected with informed consent from participants (Section 3.5), including human users, pets, and environmental motion sources.

2. Data are anonymized, with no personal identity information involved.

3. The paper discusses the non-intrusive, privacy-preserving advantages of WiFi sensing (Sections 1 and 7), making it suitable for home health monitoring and similar positive applications.

4. No major ethical risks are identified, and the work complies with NeurIPS ethics standards.

dataset_code_comments.value:
1. The dataset, code, and project website are all publicly available (linked in the abstract and Section 1), covering data collection, preprocessing, and model training pipelines.

2. The documentation is complete, supporting reproducibility and community contributions (Section 7).

3. Evaluation splits, difficulty levels, and OOD protocols are clearly defined, enabling consistent benchmarking.

additional_feedback.value:
1. If phase recovery or calibrated phase data can be introduced in future versions, it would greatly broaden the applicability of the dataset.

2. Incorporating temporally structured tasks, such as long-term health monitoring or overnight behavior sequences, would enhance practical value.

3. Consider releasing higher-level data APIs, such as PyTorch or TensorFlow Dataset wrappers, to improve usability.

4. A more systematic evaluation of how hardware configurations (e.g., bandwidth, MIMO setup) impact task performance could be helpful for deployment recommendations.

final_justification.value: The authors have mostly addressed my concerns in the rebuttal. Since my initial score was already 'Accept', I have decided to maintain this score and continue to lean toward accepting the paper.

summary.value: The paper introduces CSI-Bench as a new large-scale Wifi-CSI-based dataset that can be leveraged for various Wifi-based tasks. The main contribution is the introduction of the large-scale CSI dataset which covers a more diverse range of scenarios, equipments, and probable tasks.

strengths_contributions.value: Overall, the paper is easy to follow and the introduced CSI-bench is indeed a much larger dataset that can potentially build a pathway towards minimizing the gap between the complexity of CSI data in real-world applications versus the lack of generalizability of current datasets. The authors have cited most datasets relevant to CSI-bench with some comparisons.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Although the authors have made a good effort to create a CSI dataset, focusing on improving from past datasets by introducing variances in equipments, environments, and tasks, there is much concerns of the dataset with regards to the details of data collection, the quality of the tasks given the current benchmark results, and lack of analysis and discussion. Detailed concerns are as follows:

1. Unclear device selections and configurations: compared with prior datasets, one significant difference in CSI-bench is the inclusion of 16 different devices instead of a single device. What are the criteria for the selection of these devices? Also, as pointed out by the authors, the different devices result in very different CSI signals, and I suppose this is the reason why the different devices are used for the different tasks. It is noted that not one of the tasks leveraged on ALL 16 devices, so how are the devices actually distributed among the tasks and why are they distributed in that way? Meanwhile, how actually the devices are located and set in the different environments? This obviously would affect the actual quality of the data collected.
2. Unclear environment settings and configurations: one other significant difference in CSI-bench is the inclusion of different environments. What are the criteria of the selection of these 26 environments? Also, while it is observed that none of the environments share the same configuration (in terms of either number of floors, layout, or area), is there are quantitative way to illustrate how different these environments are? Since the authors differentiate these environments in terms of type, area, layout type, and number of floors, how are these factors contributing to the variances of CSI data collected or to the performances of the models? Additionally, what are the layouts of the environments and (as pointed out in concern 1) how are the devices located and set in each environment?
3. Other concerns in data collection and pre-processing: there are additional two concerns to raise for the data collection and pre-processing. The authors state that a user annotation tool is developed to optionally log daily activities by users, could the authors give a simple illustration of how the annotation tool is? What is the frequency of users willing to log daily activities? Further, as shown in Table 2, the settings for each task are split into easy, medium, and hard. What are the criteria that differentiates the difficulty of the data?
4. Questions over the quality (challenges) of the tasks with saturated benchmark results: the authors have reported performances of various methods, which includes very "old-school" neural networks and more "recent" transformer-based models. One concern raised after observing the results is in actually how challenging the tasks are and whether this illustrates that the trained models can be deployed in actual applications? As shown, even the most primitive neural network (MLP) can score a 85+ accuracy and F1-score in fall detection, breathing detection, room-level localization, and motion source recognition. Then it really questions whether there is a need for further research since for Transformer-based models, the average accuracy of these tasks is 96+. If the results are already saturated, why bother to still put in resource and effort in something that almost cannot improve any further?
5. Lack of analysis and discussion: last but not least, the authors only provided very limited result analysis and discussion from the benchmark results presented. As a benchmarking paper, it should be noted that providing the data itself is of limited contribution to the community. summary.value:
CSI-Bench introduces the first large-scale in-the-wild benchmark for multi-task WiFi sensing, addressing the critical gap in real-world generalization for Channel State Information (CSI)-based human monitoring.

Primary Contributions:

1.461 hours of CSI data from 35 users across 26 real environments (homes/offices/public spaces).

2.Captured via 16+ commercial devices (Qualcomm/Broadcom/Espressif/NXP) under real-world conditions (LoS/NLoS, ambient noise).

3.Includes 7 tasks: Fall/breathing detection, localization, motion source recognition, + co-labeled multi-task data (activity/user ID/proximity).

4.Hardware-agnostic preprocessing: Standardized amplitude-focused pipelines handling heterogeneous CSI formats.

5.OOD generalization protocols: Cross-user/device/environment splits to quantify real-world robustness.

6.60% parameter reduction via shared Transformer backbone + task-specific LoRA adapters.

7.validated performance gains (e.g., +12.39% accuracy in activity recognition vs. single-task).

strengths_contributions.value:
1.First large-scale in-the-wild WiFi sensing benchmark, 461+ hours, 26 diverse environments (homes/offices/public spaces), 35 users, 20 pets, and 16 commercial devices (Qualcomm/Broadcom/Espressif/NXP).

2. NLoS conditions, background interference, natural activities, and multi-device heterogeneity.

3.Joint labels for 7 tasks (fall/breathing detection, localization, motion recognition, user ID, activity, proximity), enabling parameter-efficient multi-task learning.

4.Shared Transformer backbone + task-specific LoRA adapters achieves +12.39% accuracy gain (Table 4) with lower deployment costs.

5.Hardware-agnostic preprocessing. Standardized amplitude extraction, subcarrier alignment, and CSI verification tools (MATLAB-based) ensure data reliability across chipsets.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1.The authors did not conduct an in-depth analysis of the fundamental challenges posed by hardware heterogeneity (e.g., CSI format variations across chipsets) and environmental noise (e.g., multipath effects) on model design.

2.The authors did not compare against recent multimodal WiFi datasets (e.g., MM-Fi) or robustness optimization methods (e.g., adversarial training), which should be supplemented.

3.The authors merely noted that existing works "lack unified evaluation" but failed to explain how their novel evaluation protocols (difficulty tiers/OOD splits) quantify generalization gaps.

4.Clarify the selection criteria for the 16 devices (e.g., market share basis) and include critical parameters (e.g., transmit power) in the hardware configuration table (Appendix Table 6).

5.While rightly acknowledging phase unreliability (Section 4.1), the authors did not explore new phase calibration methods (e.g., [10,30]), limiting signal utilization.

6.Detail the physical rationale (e.g., signal attenuation models) for the distance segmentation (0.5/1.5/2.5/3.5m).

7.Baselines exclusively used general time-series models without comparison against domain-specific architectures (e.g., RFNet or CSI-Net).

summary.value: This paper introduces CSI-Bench, the first large-scale in-the-wild WiFi sensing dataset aimed at addressing key challenges in the field, such as environment-controlled data collection, hardware homogeneity, and non-continuous session-based CSI signals. The dataset comprises CSI signals collected using 16 different commercial WiFi edge devices across 26 distinct environments and from 35 users. It includes multiple baselines for a range of task, including fall detection, breathing detection, localization, motion source recognition, action recognition, user identification, and proximity estimation, which are evaluated under both single-task supervised learning and multi-task learning frameworks. Overall, CSI-Bench presents a comprehensive and valuable testbed for advancing human-centric research and health monitoring applications in real-world WiFi sensing scenarios.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The dataset offers a multi-device and multi-platform framework for WiFi CSI data collection, supporting practical deployment across a variety of real-world environments. With 16 different commercial devices, it surpasses previous works in scale and heterogeneity.
2. It introduces a continuous data recording approach along with a validation tool to assess CSI signal quality, enhancing the dataset’s reliability. The inclusion of several baselines helps demonstrate the potential of WiFi sensing in various human-centered healthcare applications.
3. CSI-Bench has strong potential to promote out-of-distribution research in WiFi-based human sensing, particularly in scenarios involving cross-device and cross-environment generalization, which is an area of growing importance in real-world deployment.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. While the dataset targets health-related applications, the number of proposed healthcare-specific benchmarks is relatively limited. Tasks such as fall detection and breathing detection have already been widely explored using WiFi and other RF-based signals. To highlight the advantages of CSI data for smart healthcare, the inclusion of more novel and domain-specific tasks would be beneficial.
2. The dataset is restricted to a single modality, i.e., WiFi CSI signals, lacking complementary data such as 3D skeletal motion, textual action descriptions, or depth information, which have been included in some previous WiFi-based datasets. Incorporating such multimodal data could greatly enhance the dataset’s versatility and utility for broader research applications.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The dataset and code URLs are publicly available. Additionally, a detailed README file is provided to guide users through dataset usage and implementation, which enhances accessibility and reproducibility for the research community.

additional_feedback.value:
1. The paper mentions standardizing CSI data from different devices using zero-padding or clipping due to varying numbers of subcarriers. However, devices may also differ in the number of antennas, which can significantly affect the data structure. It would be helpful if the authors could clarify how they ensure consistency in input formatting, specifically, whether antenna subcarriers are stacked or processed separately.
2. The experimental setup would benefit from further justification regarding parameter choices. For instance, the segmentation durations of 5 and 10 seconds are not supported by statistical analysis or empirical reasoning. Furthermore, the definition of “room-level localization” remains unclear. Does it involve classifying among six pre-defined locations, or is it a regression task predicting coordinates? I believe that clarifying this distinction and illustrating how it differs from proximity recognition would help readers better understand the scope of these benchmarks.
3. The out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation results presented in the Appendix, particularly those related to cross-device generalization, are highly relevant to the core premise of the dataset being “in-the-wild.” These results would be more impactful if moved into the main paper, as they underscore the robustness and real-world applicability of the dataset.
4. While the paper frequently emphasizes health monitoring as a primary motivation, only two benchmarks (fall detection and breathing detection) are healthcare-related. Incorporating additional, meaningful health-focused tasks would better reflect the stated goals and help showcase the unique strengths of WiFi sensing in medical and assistive contexts compared to other sensing modalities.

final_justification.value: Overall, I believe this work makes a valuable contribution to the field of WiFi-based human sensing for healthcare. Thus, I plan to raise my rating to "accept".

title.value: CSI-Bench: A Large-Scale In-the-Wild Dataset for Multi-task WiFi Sensing

abstract.value:
WiFi sensing has emerged as a compelling contactless modality for human activity monitoring by capturing fine-grained variations in Channel State Information (CSI). Its ability to operate continuously and non-intrusively while preserving user privacy makes it particularly suitable for health monitoring. However, existing WiFi sensing systems struggle to generalize in real-world settings, largely due to datasets collected in controlled environments with homogeneous hardware and fragmented, session-based recordings that fail to reflect continuous daily activity.

We present CSI-Bench, a large-scale, in-the-wild benchmark dataset collected using commercial WiFi edge devices across 26 diverse indoor environments with 35 real users. Spanning over 461 hours of effective data, CSI-Bench captures realistic signal variability under natural conditions. It includes task-specific datasets for fall detection, breathing monitoring, localization, and motion source recognition, as well as a co-labeled multitask dataset with joint annotations for user identity, activity, and proximity. To support the development of robust and generalizable models, CSI-Bench provides standardized evaluation splits and baseline results for both single-task and multi-task learning. CSI-Bench offers a foundation for scalable, privacy-preserving WiFi sensing systems in health and broader human-centric applications.
